chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said:

I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a group of the enemy who made peace (sulah) but then betrayed (kharafu), and perhaps they only betrayed because justice was not done to them. Is it permissible to buy from their captives (sabiy)? He said: 'If they are from the enemy whose enmity has become clear, then buy from them; and buy from them; and if they have been displaced and were wronged, then do not buy from their captives.'

key_terms.صَالَحُوا: They made peace / concluded a treaty

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for purchasing captives from enemies who broke their peace treaty?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) refines the jurisprudence of *saby* (captivity) by introducing a qualitative distinction based on the motive behind the treaty breach: if the enemy's hostility was manifest and inherent, their captives may be purchased, but if they were displaced or wronged (*nufirū wa ẓulimū*), their captives are exempt from purchase. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on justice (*‘adl*) and intent (*niyyah*) in war, ensuring that captives are not treated merely as commodities but as individuals whose status depends on the fairness of their prior treatment. It highlights the principle that oppression or displacement can alter the legal status of a group, preventing the exploitation of those who were victims of injustice.
